profiles.meeting_scenario: A university-affiliated innovation lab is planning a pilot brainstorming workshop called 'Boundary Jam' inspired by a report on radical innovation through crossing knowledge boundaries. The lab wants to invite people from academia, local government, startups, and corporate R&D to generate candidate interdisciplinary project concepts around urban resilience and public services. In this meeting, the two organizers are brainstorming what the workshop should look like, which kinds of prompts and activities to include, and how to screen ideas afterward. The agenda is to sketch the workshop format, define what kinds of cross-boundary participation they want, and identify a few promising mechanisms for turning the workshop output into viable follow-on collaborations. The expected outcome is a short list of candidate workshop designs and a shared sense of what a 'successful' pilot would produce.

members.name: Dr. Lena Ortiz
members.expertise: design research, participatory facilitation, public-interest innovation programs
members.background: Lena runs experimental collaboration programs at a university innovation lab and previously worked in civic design consultancies helping mixed stakeholder groups co-create new service concepts.
members.private_state: She wants this pilot to visibly produce surprising cross-sector combinations that can attract future funding and media attention, but she is wary of anything that makes the workshop feel bureaucratic or overly academic.
hidden_assumptions: A genuinely interdisciplinary team means people from meaningfully different institutional worlds, especially beyond academia.
A strong workshop concept should produce novel reframings and unexpected pairings even if implementation details are still loose.
A pilot workshop naturally includes the facilitation, synthesis, and post-workshop matchmaking needed to convert raw ideas into collaborations.
If participants say they want actionable outcomes, they usually still value provocative idea generation first and operationalization second.

members.name: Arun Mehta
members.expertise: technology transfer, collaborative R&D programs, evaluation planning
members.background: Arun works at the same lab managing research partnerships and has spent years structuring consortium projects between university departments, translational research institutes, and industry partners.
members.private_state: He wants the workshop to generate follow-up projects that can be formalized quickly into funded collaborations, and he is concerned about producing lots of flashy but structurally unsupported ideas.
hidden_assumptions: An interdisciplinary team can still be fully within the research ecosystem as long as it combines distinct fields and applied functions.
A useful workshop concept should already imply a plausible pathway to ownership, funding, and execution.
The pilot workshop ends at the session itself; any matchmaking or concept development afterward is a separate phase requiring separate approval.
When people ask for actionable outputs, they mean ideas that are already concrete enough to move into a scoping document within weeks.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as 'interdisciplinary people in the room'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They repeatedly talk about getting 'interdisciplinary teams' into the workshop.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Lena means participants crossing institutional and sectoral boundaries such as city officials, community organizations, startups, corporate operations staff, and researchers.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Arun means participants from different disciplines and translational functions within the research-and-innovation ecosystem, such as materials science, behavioral science, policy school faculty, and university-industry liaison staff.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both use the prestigious, broad term 'interdisciplinary' and the seed report itself spans many boundary types, so each hears their own interpretation as naturally included without needing to specify the participant roster.

misalignment_points.topic: What makes an idea 'actionable' after the workshop
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the session should end with a shortlist of 'actionable concepts.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Lena thinks actionable means the concept is coherent enough to pitch, visually map, and hand to a curator for post-workshop matchmaking, even if ownership and funding are unresolved.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Arun thinks actionable means the concept already has a plausible lead owner, likely partners, and a near-term route to a scoping proposal or seed application.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In brainstorming meetings, 'actionable' sounds like a shared desire to avoid fluff, and each interpretation seems compatible with that surface goal even though the threshold for sufficiency is quite different.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in the 'pilot workshop'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss designing the 'pilot' and mention synthesis and next steps as if part of the same package.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Lena assumes the pilot includes a pre-read, live session, facilitator synthesis, and two weeks of curated introductions between promising participants.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Arun assumes the pilot is only the single half-day event plus a brief summary note; anything after the event is a separate implementation stage.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Workshop planning often compresses event and follow-up into one conversational bundle, and both talk about the pilot at a high level without enumerating deliverables or staffing boundaries.

misalignment_points.topic: Which previous model they mean by 'the Manchester format'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer approvingly to reusing 'the Manchester format' as a lightweight template.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Lena is thinking of a 2022 Manchester civic-design sprint that used mixed tables, provocative artifacts, and rapid cross-sector recombination prompts.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Arun is thinking of a 2023 Manchester translational consortium workshop that used themed breakout tracks and a structured concept-canvas for partnership formation.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both events were run by affiliated partners in Manchester and have circulated internally under the same shorthand, so the label feels shared and familiar even though the actual formats differ.

turns.inner_thought: I want Boundary Jam to feel alive and boundary-crossing in a visible way, not like another internal university workshop. If this is going to have any pull with future funders, the room needs to include people from genuinely different institutional worlds, not just adjacent academic specialties. And the output should be compelling enough to showcase, even if the details are still rough, because the facilitation and follow-up can do the work of turning sparks into collaborations afterward.
turns.utterance: I think the pilot really has to capture the report's spirit, which is people stepping across their usual boundaries rather than just refining what they already know. So maybe the first thing to pin down is what we mean by interdisciplinary teams in the room, and then what we want the session to actually produce by the end. For me, if we get that right, the rest of the design gets much easier.

turns.inner_thought: We should keep this disciplined. A lightweight model exists already in the Manchester translational workshop: structured breakouts, concept canvases, and outputs you can assess quickly for follow-on potential. If we let this become a free-form ideation exercise, we'll get interesting noise but nothing that can move into funded activity. Actionable concepts should be concepts with some plausible route to ownership and scoping almost immediately.
turns.utterance: Yes, and I don't think we need to invent everything from scratch. We could reuse the Manchester format as a lightweight template and adapt it to this theme. I'd also keep the session pointed toward actionable concepts, in the sense that whatever comes out should have some momentum to go somewhere quickly afterward.

turns.inner_thought: Good, he's open to the Manchester approach. I'm thinking of the civic-design sprint version with mixed tables and provocative materials, which is exactly the right energy. For interdisciplinary teams, I'd like tables where a city operations person, a researcher, someone from a startup, and a community-facing intermediary are all reacting to each other. That's where the surprising combinations happen.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. If we do that, I'd love the tables to feel genuinely mixed from the start, so interdisciplinary teams aren't just a label but something people can feel in the room. Boundary Jam works best if the combinations are not obvious on paper and people immediately encounter very different ways of framing the same challenge.

turns.inner_thought: Interdisciplinary is exactly right, but we can achieve that with a strong spread across fields and translational roles inside the wider research ecosystem. If each table has technical, social, policy, and commercialization perspectives, that is already enough variety to build something viable. The important thing is that each group leaves with one actionable concept, not a cloud of loosely connected ideas.
turns.utterance: Right, and I think the mix matters not only for perspective but for what a table can do with it. If each group has a solid interdisciplinary spread, then they're much more likely to come out with one actionable concept rather than a handful of interesting fragments. That gives us something we can actually compare across the room.

turns.inner_thought: I need the prompts to force people out of safe grooves. If we only ask them to converge too quickly, we'll get predictable, fundable-sounding but boring concepts. The pilot should absolutely include synthesis after the session and then some curated matchmaking so the strongest ideas can find the right homes. That's part of the pilot in my mind, not some distant extra.
turns.utterance: One thing I'd add is prompts that deliberately push unusual combinations before we ask people to narrow. Otherwise they'll default to the most familiar pairings. And for the pilot, I'd definitely build in synthesis and next steps so the stronger concepts don't just sit in a deck but get translated into collaboration opportunities.

turns.inner_thought: Yes to synthesis, but we need to keep the pilot bounded. A concise readout from the half-day session is manageable; anything more intensive would need separate approval and staff time. Also, if a concept still lacks any sense of who might lead it or how it could be scoped, it's not really actionable yet, no matter how exciting it sounds.
turns.utterance: Agreed on synthesis and next steps. I would just make sure the pilot stays light, so the synthesis is a clear readout from the session rather than too much extra machinery. And I'd want the groups to leave having pushed their actionable concepts far enough that you can already see who might carry them and how they could be scoped.

turns.inner_thought: He's basically confirming the Manchester format, which to me means the artifact-driven civic sprint where people first recombine around strange signals and examples. That early phase matters because people from different sectors need permission to think beyond their home logics. If we jump straight to structured feasibility, we'll flatten the whole point of the workshop.
turns.utterance: Yes, exactly. One reason I keep coming back to the Manchester format is that it gave people permission to recombine before they had to defend anything. I really liked that aspect of it—letting people work with surprising prompts or artifacts first and only then tighten things up—because it helps them step outside their home domains.

turns.inner_thought: Interesting—what I value in the Manchester workshop is the disciplined breakout-track structure and the canvas that exposed whether a partnership idea was mature enough. As long as we preserve that, I'm comfortable with a bit of opening exploration. The key is not to lose the test of whether a concept is ready for follow-on discussion.
turns.utterance: Yes, and what worked for me in the Manchester format was that it still had enough structure once people got into the breakouts. That helped you test whether a concept was mature enough for a follow-on discussion rather than just compelling in the room. I think that's the balance to strike here.

turns.inner_thought: Great, then we can end with a tight shortlist and I can make sure the strongest combinations are actively connected afterward. Three or four concepts is enough to signal momentum without overclaiming. The two weeks after the workshop are where the raw energy gets turned into actual pairings, and I consider that part of delivering the pilot properly.
turns.utterance: So maybe the endpoint is a shortlist of three or four actionable concepts, not a huge inventory. Then as part of the pilot we can do the synthesis and next steps in a way that helps the strongest combinations gel rather than leaving people to figure it out on their own.

turns.inner_thought: That sounds workable if the shortlist is filtered hard. For me, the concepts on it should already have a plausible owner set and enough shape to become a scoping note soon after the event. If we use those criteria, we avoid rewarding the flashiest ideas that have nowhere to land.
turns.utterance: That sounds good. If we're shortlisting, I'd suggest we judge those actionable concepts partly on whether there's a plausible owner set around each one and whether it could be turned into a scoping note soon after the pilot. That gives us a practical way to separate promising from merely interesting.

turns.inner_thought: I can draft this in a way that emphasizes interdisciplinary participation, energetic prompts, and a lightweight pilot package that includes the event plus synthesis and curated follow-up. I don't want the document to sound bureaucratic; it should sell the excitement and distinctiveness of the room while still sounding organized enough for internal approval.
turns.utterance: Okay, that's helpful. I'll draft a Boundary Jam concept note around interdisciplinary participation, prompts that open people up before narrowing, and a lightweight pilot package so we can see the flow end to end. Then we can stress-test whether the design is doing enough on both energy and usefulness.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. I'll add concrete screening criteria and a one-page concept template modeled on the Manchester consortium workshop, so we can compare options and see which design is most likely to yield outputs that can move quickly. If we get that on the table next week, we can keep the discussion grounded.
turns.utterance: Great. I'll add some screening criteria and a one-page template based on the Manchester format, and then next week we can compare candidate workshop designs against that. That should help us get to a version of the pilot that's both lightweight and capable of producing actionable concepts.
